segments.text: Blockchain-Integrated Lightweight Machine Learning Framework for Real-Time Threat Detection in IoT Networks Abstract:
segments.label: human

segments.text: The explosive growth of IoT networks has raised stakes for cyber threats, demanding effective, scalable and powerful systems to detect them. This paper introduces a new Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) model using edge computing, which combines the blockchain technology and lightweight Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to protect the IoT environment. The solution adopts the decision tree (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors, to carry out on-the-fly energy-efficient threat classification that tackles limitation of resources in IoT. Features are extracted and dimensions reduced using PCA so that accurate detection with low overhead can be performed. A simplified blockchain is provided to securely record and log network activity and threat events, as while smart contracts automate responses to threats like isolating infected devices or alerting administrators. For low-latency, we deploy Machine Learning (ML) models to the edge of the network for on-premise reasoning, which can quickly detect and mitigate malware. In addition, adaptive model retraining based on periodically aggregated edge data provides robustness against shifting threat patterns. The Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework presents several advantages, such as secure and unmutated logging, real-time actioning as well as scalability for large IoT networks with a classification accuracy over 95%. Featuring the simplicity of traditional ML algorithms as well as the tamper-resistance of blockchain, our solution provides a practical and efficient mechanism to protect IoT networks against new cyber threats.

segments.label: human

segments.text: The rapid development of the so called Internet of Things (IoT) brought innovations to industries enabling them by providing seamless connectivity, automation [1]. Nevertheless, all these huge interconnected device networks are under increasing threat from cyber security attacks like unauthorized access or malware infiltration Secure intelligent fuzzy blockchain framework Efficient threat detection in iot networks [2]. Traditional threat surveillance does not cope well with the specific requirements of IoT ecosystems such as limited available computation, and dynamics within the threat landscape. Mitigating these challenges is now an open problem which calls for novel solutions that deliver efficiency, scalability and resiliency to provide security in IoT networks while maintaining their operational effectiveness and real-time reactivity [3]. Advances in blockchain and machine learning (ML) technologies have the potential to revolutionize IoT security [4]. Blockchains offer a decentralized and immutable infrastructure for secure logging of data and automatic action, with lightweight ML methods providing efficient threat detection with low computational impact [5]. The principles underlying these technologies are well-suited to the unique demands of constrained IoT devices, which
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: suggests that they could provide a route to trustworthy and scalable security solutions. The convergence of blockchain and ML can be seen as opening up a new path to strengthen the security of IoT networks in the era of cyber threats. The distinct computational limitations associated with the IoT devices, require a novel form of rethinking when it comes to traditional cybersecurity formalisms [6]. Contrary to traditional networks, in IoT attack detection has to find a trade off between intensive possession and computation of small amount power and bandwidth. This dual challenge mandates the need for lightweight frameworks that can quickly classify and mitigate threats with minimal impact on the underlying hardware [7]. From feature~extraction methods to efficient machine learning (ML) models sitting on top of a single secure blockchain layer, a holistic security profile for IoT scenarios is provided [8]. The proposed Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework provides solutions for these challenges by combining the decentralized ledger technology with ML algorithms, that were designed to work in real time.

segments.text: The decision trees (DT) and K-nearest neighbors (KNN) offer efficient threat classification, whereas principal component analysis (PCA) contributes to accurate feature extraction in a computationally lightweight manner. Smart contract enabled automated threat responses improve network immunity. Edge-based deployment of machine learning (ML) cuts the latency by half, which makes all IoT networks to be secured and functioning in real time. 1.1 Background The emergence of IoT networks has provided new possibilities for automation and connectivity in many industries, but also exposes potential vulnerabilities to cybersecurity challenges. Mainstream security mechanisms cannot effectively cope with the rapidly growing IoT environments that are diverse in size and resource availability. The combination of blockchain and light-weight machine learning (ML) can be utilized for this problem despite the previously mentioned limitations, providing decentralized, secure and efficient threat detection mechanisms specifically designed for IoT. 1.2 Scope and Motivation The Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) is a scalable and light-weight resource real-time IoT network security framework. The product incorporates light-weight machine-learning (ML) models for edge-based threat detection, a blockchain data-logger and automated outreach responses. The cyber attacks towards IoT networks are growing in number and sophistication, which can compromise the integrity, confidentiality and availability of the connected nodes. Such requirements for lightweight and computationally efficient security solutions comply with the limitations of IoT devices, inspiring the design in this paper of LB-TD: Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection. 1.3 Objectives and Key Contributions
segments.label: human

segments.text: The main objective of this research is to design a secure, effective and scalable threat detection solution which can be accomplished using blockchain and lightweight ML algorithms. The model maintains constant monitoring capabilities, secure loggings that cannot be erased and self-customized to defend against ever-changing cyber attacks. The main novel contributions of this paper are: ➢​ Development of the Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework which fuses LP-Machine learning algorithms and blockchain for secure and efficient detection of threats in IoT networks. ➢​ Real-time threat classification with low computational overhead based on Decision Trees (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN).
segments.label: human

segments.text: ➢​ Using PCA for feature extraction and dimensionality reduction to improve the detection accuracy. ➢​ Inclusion of a lightweight blockchain for non-repudiation logging and automatic smart contract-driven threat responses. 1.4 Organization of the paper The paper is structured as follows: the Related Works section examines existing approaches to IoT security and highlights gaps addressed by the proposed framework. The Methodology details the design and implementation of the Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework, including the integration of blockchain and machine learning (ML) components. The Experimentation section outlines the evaluation setup, datasets, and performance metrics. Results discuss the framework’s performance, including accuracy, latency, and scalability. The paper concludes with insights, limitations, and potential directions for future research.

For traditional algorithms, imbalanced class is still a challenging issue, e.g., benign traffic of orders of magnitude more than malicious samples, thus the relatively low detection accuracy for rare attack categories. Moreover, deep learning models are too computationally expensive to be deployed in resource-constrained IoT devices (the enablers of real-time threat detection in dynamic environments). These solutions do not even begin to address the privacy issues surrounding sensitive data in decentralized systems Our Privacy Continuum Many existing systems built for distributed computation struggle to maintain user privacy. These constraints severely limit one's capability to design and deploy large-scale, cost-effective and secure intrusion detection systems for IoT networks. Table 1 summarises the research gaps based on review of literature. Our model mitigates the issues of class imbalance and limited labelled data based on a decentralized anomaly detection framework using Swarm Learning to perform local data fusion. Such design can make sure that sensitive data are kept in local devices, and thus will protect users' privacy without a requirement of centralized data storage. To alleviate the computational burden of these IoT devices, they resort to knowledge distillation that compresses the detection model size without loss in accuracy. Thanks to local edge computing, the model can reduce latency and enhance scalability making it suitable for resource-constrained IoT scenarios. It is also worth mentioning that the ongoing learning mechanism enables the model to keep up with novel attack patterns without wasting resources. 3. METHODOLOGY The approach that we propose is based on a decentralized model for Anomaly Detection in IoT networks, and issues related to the scarcity of labeled data when applying such models to unknown scenarios. It combines Swarm Learning (SL) to allow local data fusion among

It contains benign and malignant samples that represent several IoT attack scenarios of different types. segments.text: ​ 3.1.1 Dataset Description The Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity Intrusion Detection System (CICIDS) 2017 Dataset is also a Kaggle dataset that contains more than 80GB of network data divided between training and test sets. About 70% of the data, roughly 1,200,000 samples is used for training and remaining 30%, approximately 500,000 samples would be for testing. The dataset comprises several attributes such as flow-duration, packets counts, protocol types, bytes counts and connection flags and service types. It stands for a wide range of attack types such as DoS, DDoS, Brute-Force, Port Scans and Injections. With the training and test sets composed of normal traffic apparently suitable for model learning as well as more suspicious labeled or even attack traffic (if ever occurring at all), this dataset is a good choice for both training and evaluating anomaly detection models in IoT security use cases. 3.2 Data Preprocessing Data preprocessing is an essential process to guarantee the good quality and accuracy of machine learning models in network traffic datasets, such as the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity Intrusion Detection System (CICIDS) 2017. segments.text: 3.3 Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) Framework
segments.label: human

segments.text: Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection The LB-TD architecture depicted in Figure 2 is organized into three specific layers, namely Edge, Blockchain and Cloud/Server which perform peculiar role with respect to the real-time threat detection within IoT networks.
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: The approach, shown in Figure 2, aims to reduce computation cost of IoT devices for log generation and secure recording of network activity while it scales up for large scale IoT.
segments.label: human

segments.text: Figure 2: Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) Framework 3.3.1 Edge Layer (IoT Devices) In the Edge Layer, local threat detection on IOT devices is achieved using lightweight machine learning models. The role of the edge layer is that it should enable to classify network traffic and device behavior in real time with limited delay. IoT Things typically involve very limited computational and power resources. As a result, lightweight algorithms, such as Decision Trees (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), are used to achieve fast and effective malicious traffic detection. These are trained to identify patterns associated with identified threats, and because they are computationally cheap, these can be distributed on edge devices which have poor processing power and memory. At this layer, the received inputs from IoT devices—sensor values, traffic probabilities and device access logs—are transformed.
segments.label: human

segments.text: The PCA (Principal Component Analysis) is used for the data dimensionality reduction, which makes the input data compact and with satisfactory description ability for radians measurement values reconstruction. When the data is analyzed, the low-overhead machine learning models categorize whether a device or traffic flow are acting in regular fashion or presenting suspicious behaviors typical of cybercrime. The edge devices, when they find a potential threat, do not act on their own. Instead they make an entry of the event locally and interface with the Blockchain Layer to add these findings to the permanent ledger enabling a transparent approach for accountability in detection.

segments.text: 3.3.2 Blockchain Layer
segments.label: human

segments.text: The Blockchain Layer is the underpinning of secure and immutable network activity logging and threat event logging. To that end, CTR employs a lightweight blockchain to record the

segments.text: detection event, ie. device IDs, timestamps, threat scores and of course the type of threat detected (e.g., denial-of-service attempt, malware infection..). This layer helps preserve data recorded in the system and makes it tamper prevention, against attackers that may want to change or delete detection logs and disrupt system transparency and trust. Furthermore, smart contracts are used in the blockchain to automatically make responses against detected threats. For instance, if the cloud-based computing system detects a suspected threat, one or more particular threat countermeasure devices can be immediately isolated from the network using respective smart contracts.
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: The smart contract can also store the demitigation that has been made, providing a proven record to all responses initiated against found threats. The blockchain architecture enables distributed consensus mechanisms that allow for all devices in the IoT to reach consensus on the veracity of recorded threat events and mitigation actions. Not having a central node provides fault tolerance and further improves the stability of Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) system. Blockchain transactions being immutable also offer an audit trail, which can be leveraged for post-incident or forensic analysis. 3.3.3 Cloud/Server Layer The Cloud/Server Layer compiles the data from the edge devices over time to conduct periodical retraining of machine learning models. Since the edge devices are constantly observing and logging traffic in the network, local detection of threats and network data at each device is forwarded to a main cloud server for further inspection. This accumulation enables curricula renewal, or re‐retraining of models according to recently gathered data from various origins in the IoT world. The cloud layer also acts as a springboard for world-wide threat analysis. Here, the information received from different IoT devices is integrated to identify higher level attack signatures that are difficult to identify from a single device perspective. For example, coordinated IoT attacks may be detected as diverse data is combined and jointly processed. Additionally, the cloud layer updates and re-trains these light-weight machine learning models with the aggregated data so that the system can grow according to changing threats and network features. This is to maintain the effectiveness of the models at detecting known and new types of attacks. The retrained models are uploaded to the edge devices for local realtime detection. Also, this layer is the platform on which manual or administrative steps are taken against serious or impenetrable threats. Sys admins can be notified via the blockchain’s smart contracts, or centralised dashboards that show the IoT network current status.

segments.text: 3.3.4 Integration Between Layers ➢​ Flow of Data: When data is generated from IoT devices, it goes through the data flow in order to be placed into the blockchain layer and securely recorded. The logged data could be aggregated and examined in the cloud-server for worldwide perception and model retraining. ➢​ Real-Time Operations: working in real-time the effects of threats can be discovered instantly. Uses are if something happens, it immediately gets recorded and logged on the blockchain to have that happened in a tamper proofing way as well authorize action by other systems through smart contracts. ➢​ Scalable: The model is scalable for pervasive IOT networks. Edge computing is employed to process the most data on site while relieving the central cloud infrastructure as much as possible. The blockchain layer could not only guarantee the security of threat logs, but also the computation overhead is acceptable. This three layers architecture presents an inbuilt approach of defence against threats, by combining real time processing on edge, secure and transparent logging through blockchain, and scalability/versatility from cloud/server layer. The LB-TD framework prevents low-latency threat detection, hard data logging, and adaptive threat mitigation in a large-scale IoT network. 3.4 Development of Machine Learning Models The model of LB-TD The lightweight blockchain-based threat detection (LB-TD) framework uses two lightweight machine learning algorithms, Decision Trees (DT) and K -Nearest Neighbors (KNN), which are appropriate for resource-constrained environments. The models were chosen because they are computationally efficient, interpretable and effective at detecting anomalous activities in IoT networks. 3.4.1 Decision Trees (DT) The simple logic to the decision processes appeals to us, as they depends on dividing subsets of data based on features used and the majority in them. Such a classification hierarchy is particularly useful for the detection of malicious activity in this context, providing a transparent and interpretable path to decision making. Consider the application of IoT networks, where there are a lot of different patterns in data and DecisionTrees (DT) model that can be transparent about their decision making and thus allow administrators to check why an instance was classified as such. A decision tree works by recursively splitting the data according to feature values, where internal nodes in such trees correspond to decision rules and leaf nodes reveal the class label (malicious as opposed to benign) of a record. Decision Tree, attributed to its roots in Information Gain based decision making with quantity as Gini impurity or Entropy. After the
segments.label: human

segments.text: reduction of features with PCA, we train the decision tree to judge whether an IoT device’s performance is as normal network or uncertain threat. One of the advantages of decision tree methods is its simplicity: only if-else comparisons at each node are necessary. This feature of Decision Tree (DT) renders it extremely attractive for real-time threat detection due to its ability to classify newly observed instances very quickly, even on resource-limited edge devices. segments.text: 3.4.2 K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is yet another simplistic algorithm, selected due to its ability to learn the outliers as it is based on distance from closest point in feature space. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) – New instance is to be classified based on its proximity to the k-nearest instances (neighbors?) in the training dataset. The new point is classified according to the most frequent class of its k-nearest neighbors. This approach works in sparse or high variance data such as most of the IoT networks where network traffic and device behavior can be significantly different. In this structure, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) works by measuring the distance (typically Euclidean or Manhattan) between the input features of a new sample and features of previously supported instances. Afterwards, the point is assigned a label that corresponds to its most common among nearest neighbors. Specifically, as a type of abnormal detection approach, KNN is well adapted to anomaly detection as it compares new data with two profiles about normal and attack behaviors for recognition of outlierness different from the normal or attack pattern. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is simple and needs very few computations, it is therefore well adapted for implementation on the edge devices that has limited resources in terms of computation and power. Also, due to K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)’s capability on complex decision boundaries, it is likely to be useful for finding minor anomalies from normal pattern which might lead to sophisticated attack. The two models are tested on a validation set and classification accuracy, precision, recall and F1- score used as detection metrics between normal and attack instances. 3.4.4 Edge Deployment After training, the Decision Tree and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) models are deployed to edge devices in the IoT network, enabling real-time localized threat classification. The implementation ensures that IoT nodes can classify shell traffic and node behaviour without direct link to a centralized cloud treatment. This is important to stay latency low and detect-thenticate immediately potential threats. In the edge deployment, the trained classifiers are pruned and quantized to be light weight for computation and memory efficient to be run on IoT devices. For instance, first level trees are pruned to limit their depth and the number of decision nodes which in turn reduces the cost of computation for each classification. Also, in case of K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), you can use a pre-computed list of nearest neighbors or reduced number of the features to make the performance enhancement on edge-device. These models are pushed down to the edge devices where the device constantly keeps track of network traffic and its own performance, classifying incoming data in real time. Once a PonTap device finds a threat, it alerts further steps — such as writing the case on blockchain and/or resolving an action using smart contract, without resorting to anything central server.

segments.text: The use of edge models also enables scalability. When adding more IoT devices to the network, each device has ability to locally process data and perform on–device threat classification which allows to distribute computations from centralized systems. Since the models are deployed directly at the edge, they can work in environments where connectivity is poor and be used for threat detection during network outages. 3.5 Blockchain Integration for Secure Logging and Smart Contracts In LB-TD mechanism, we use lightweight blockchain to securely log the threat detection and maintain the integrity of all network activities in IoT environments. Blockchains, such as Ethereum or Hyperledger Fabric are chosen to serve as immutable, transparent and decentralized ledgers. These services scale well, allowing secure logging of threat events for even large IoT networks distributed across a wide geographic area. The fundamental purpose of incorporating blockchain is to maintain an immutable ledger of all actions so nothing, neither threats discovered, device status nor response can be forged even by a compromised node or a bad actor. This ensures openness, responsibility but also reliability of the IoT in cases of security incidents. The system contains also smart contracts for automated security responses. Automatic quarantine of devices at risk is one purpose. If a device is detected compromised though the threat detection, the smart contract can trigger the device isolation from IoT network. This self-healing action prevents continued malicious operations from the affected device, with minimal impact on the entire network. The isolation is to prevent the device from communicating on-network, place the device in a restricted network area or block its access to shared resources while still contain and inhibit its threat influence to other devices. This rapid response is important in the real-time act of threat control. A tamper-proof record of every threat event is a significant benefit as well. Each of these threats is securely recorded onto the blockchain (along with its classification, evidences, related device identifiers and timestamps as well as any further appropriate mitigation actions taken – such as isolating a device or triggering an alert).

This hybrid approach of secure logging and smart contract automation will form a robust, scalable, transparent approach to addressing IoT security threats. 3.6 Real-Time Threat Detection and Mitigation in IoT Networks Using Edge Computing and Blockchain Integration In the LB-TD framework, The edge devices in an IoT network host the machine learning models for detecting and mitigating threats in real time. These edge devices analyze the incoming

segments.text: network traffic and sensor data in order to classify potential threats using the Decision Trees (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) models that have been pre-trained. Each approach produces a threat score, which is compared against predetermined risk ranges. The threats are categorised as high, medium or low risk in the classification system. Once the risk level of a threat rises above a certain threshold, it will trigger smart contracts to be executed automatically in order to take action to alleviate the situation such as isolating devices that have fallen into the exploited state or merely notify of some event to an operator. The edge-based system allows for these decisions to be made autonomously and with as little delay as possible, free from depending on the centralised cloud infrastructure in order to minimise any time-critical threat response. The combination of distributed processing and real time response is important for ensuring the security and integrity of IoT networks, particularly in a context where threats are constantly changing. 4. EXPERIMENTATION The empirical evaluation of the LB-TD framework is conducted in the experimentation phase, to show how well our mechanism can detect and mitigate threats in an IoT network. The main target is related to evaluate the performance of lightweight machine learning models (such as Decision Tree (DT) and K- Nearest Neighbors(KNN)) in classifying threats to edge devices in the real-time. The accuracy, latency and the capability of system to adapt to new threats were tested against a set of fictive IoT environments with different network topologies and threat scenarios. Performance analysis is performed with regards to classification accuracy and the time spent in responding to a detected network attack, as well as how its performance compares when confronted with security events occurring throughout the network with short notice so that they can be mitigated accordingly. 4.1 Experimental setup The experimental system consists of hardware and software parts. The IoT hardware is a network of IoT devices such as temperature sensors, smart cameras and routers interconnected in an emulated IoT environment. Lightweight machine learning models for threat detection were deployed on edge devices (i.e., Raspberry Pi's). And on the software end, the system runs with Python based machine learning model training and inference while integrating securely with Hyperledger Fabric’s blockchain. Solidity is used to program the smart contracts and an Ethereum blockchain provides secure event logging. The edge devices also communicate with the blockchain via a minimal, local network infrastructure to provide quick realtime data transmission and action responses. 4.2 Results Research findings of this study will show that the proposed Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework can efficiently detect and neutralize IoT threats. Extensive performance evaluations were also conducted with multiple threat detection schemes and the
